Energy insiders understand the patterns well. The rate of change in the financials is the deciding factor in the long run. The rate of change for green tech is substantially stronger than that of oil - as oil is a mature technology. Green energy costs continue to drop substantially every year, oil energy cost efficiency has not substantially improved for decades.

Even as the oil industry continues to push exploration and expansion into as many new markets as possible, the inevitability of declining prices for green tech is already being felt. It will be a similar pattern to the cable TV industry - as TV via the internet has grown, end users simply walk away from rising cable costs and obtain substitute entertainment via the internet directly. So it will be with the energy industry - end users will simply start to provide their own energy via green sources directly - walking away from ever increasing costs of oil related energy. Like coal, there will always be some use for oil, but it is likely we have already reached the tipping point on growth in the oil industry.

On the hydro - yes exactly - you can build the coal plant right beside the steel plant if you want to - but the optimal hydro is restricted by geography. There is a cost benefit analysis that applies to these choices.

Your first point about supplementing power from clean sources - that's what we are doing now with a lot of the solar and wind generating capacity - these systems went in without batteries - solar is good because it often generates maximum output in sync with peak demand - wind not so much - wind at night time is energy lost (we do have massive surplus electricity at night, that is mostly currently discarded due to a lack of demand, and a lack of storage - this is now being partly addressed by Pumped Storage hydrogeneration - whereby you drain the dam to make energy in the daytime, and use energy at night to pump the water back uphill. The cost in energy lost is 15% - but the price of energy at night is nearly free, and the sale price in the day is usually much higher than 15%. It works.

To see a working example of this - go look at the Niagara Falls expansions, and the additional pumped storage capacity that has been added to those facilities.
